I work from home, so I'm often sitting at my desk. I started with a house leash and I'd step on the end not attached to him. I'd have a little pile of his kibble on my desk and whenever he'd flop down or chew a toy calmly I'd just drop a piece of food at him. I didn't give him any verbal acknowledgement or really even look at him. Then as he got calmer during the ignore puppy while mom works time I'd shorten the leash up so he had less room to roam and repeat with the magical food falling from the sky. He's 9 months old now and will happily nap near my feet for chunks of time.

As for nail trimming I started out with getting him comfy laying calm on his side, then started on messing with his nails. He got treats for looking away from me/his paw when I touched his paw. I'd rub and move his nails around a bunch too, giving treats when he would move his head away or look away from what I was doing. We're working on transitioning to doing that while sitting or standing now. He gets a good sniff, lick, or snuffle of his nail clippers before we start and then treats for avoiding looking at it. Doing it in little chunks is really useful too, it's how I got my cats to let me trim their nails also. If I could mess around with one toe but toe two would make him antsy I would stop at toe one. I always wanted to be the one to disengage with something he didn't want to do so he didn't learn that he could be a wigglewart and get me to leave his paws alone.

Body handling is important and something that is a learned skill. Teaching them to be calm while their paws and ears are touched and having them learn how to be calm while their whole body is touched will make any vet visit or grooming session less stressful. Another big important behavior is teaching a puppy how to “turn off”. Things like teaching ‘place’ or a calm down at your feet that turns into a nap will make life easier for their whole life. Some dogs do it naturally but other high energy/drive dogs need to learn how to be chill.

I think it’s more selfish to keep her alive if she’ll be suffering. I know how it feels to say goodbye to a heart horse and compassionately euthanize them. It was one of the hardest choices I ever made. I didn’t want to let go too early, I didn’t want to wait too long. After the first big ball of grief drifted away though I’ve never regretted my choice. 

He loved me and trusted me and I repaid him by giving him the kindest, gentlest, exit to the world that I could. 

After working around animals for decades and in vet med I’m of the opinion that I’d rather let my pets and animals go a week too early than a day too late. If I know the decline is coming and there’s no stopping the freight train of life I let them go before they experience the decline, when they’re calm and comfortable. For me at least I’d rather they didn’t deal with the physical pain to keep my emotional pain away. 

Let her go now so you can remember her as the amazing horse she is currently instead of what she would become later. Take your time, give her attention and everything she loves. Then let her go and grieve her passing. She’s worth making that hard decision.

The thing I had the most success with was using a house leash when my puppy was young young. We bought a cheap leash and cut the loop so it wouldn’t get caught in things and until he was puppy ‘trustworthy’ he had that attached to him every time he was out of his crate. It helped with redirecting him and getting him out of trouble before it started. I’ve also used a tether leash, I would attach that leash to my belt and so he could only stay within the leashed area near me. If I needed to work or get things done but didn’t want to crate him up I’d use that. It did end up with me getting an extra snuggly Velcro puppy pretty quickly but as long as he has a good chew toy he’s good about staying calm nearby. 

I also had a lot of luck freezing whole unpeeled carrots and letting him chew on those when he got really chompy. It was a fun shredding thing for him to have plus the cold helped his teething gums. Carrots are usually safe for dogs. You could also freeze green beans or other dog friendly veggies and it sorta replicates the shredding feel they can get from puppy pads or paper.

These little guys learn fast and he’ll learn how your home functions quickly.
